extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal principles governing the content, disclosure, and form of a patent specification (enablement, claim scope, drawings, best mode, and avoidances of misleading or overbroad language), illustrated by case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency for a skilled mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be sufficient for a mechanic, properly instructed, to make the machine or produce the manufacture described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly illustrated by cases (e.g., jury findings that the specification 'is sufficient for a mechanic, properly instructed, to make a machine'). If a skilled workman cannot construct the invention from the specification plus drawings, the patent is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim more or less than the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee 'must not only claim neither more nor less than his own invention' and must avoid appearing to appropriate any part which is old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old and immaterial parts should be omitted or expressly designated as old; otherwise construction will be against the patentee as seeking to monopolize more than he invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify known/old parts vs. new parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Those parts that are old and immaterial should either not be mentioned or should be named only to be designated as old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safest practice: describe the whole subject and then point out which parts are old and well known so the public is not misled into thinking old features are newly invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, overbroad words like 'other materials' without context
rubrics_metrics.description: Using phrases such as 'any other substance' or 'other materials may be used' can render a specification insufficient if read as overbroad beyond what the specification supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Ciegg gas apparatus — generic 'other substances' nearly fatal; court will interpret such words in light of the specification and what practical men then treated as usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims/description to materials/modes actually known to work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification implies applicability to substances or methods not then known to be usable for the specified purpose, the patentee cannot be required to foresee later successful uses; the words should be understood as referring to materials then known to be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Tenterden's approach: interpret 'other substances' as those known at the time to be available for the purpose, not everything which will burn in some sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not list many alternatives when only one will work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification states many salts/materials/methods and only one will produce the intended effect, the specification is incorrect and may invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Winter's specification listing many salts when only one worked; Derosne v. Fairie where omission about extractive step caused problems; courts presume such multiplicity may mislead the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainest and easiest mode must be disclosed (enablement in most practical form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must point out the plainest and most easy way of producing what he claims and make the public acquainted with the mode he adopts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidlitz powder case: if recipes produce ingredients that are available commercially, making the specification look like an elaborate essential process misleads and is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode / disclose most beneficial known variant
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor knows, before procuring the patent, a mode of making the manufacture more beneficial than that specified, failure to disclose it renders the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: omitting use of tallow in tempering steel trusses, or concealing aqua fortis in making verdigris, led to patents being held void; any advantageous detail known to inventor should be disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No concealment of advantageous, known alterations (even if slight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any alteration known to the inventor before obtaining the grant, however insignificant, must be disclosed; concealment raises presumption of fraudulent non-disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by lace machine example where bending teeth improved speed; concealment of such improvements can vitiate the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing unnecessary or unused parts to mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of things never used by the patentee, or unnecessary parts, will be presumed introduced to overload and mislead and may invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Arkwright's machine and others where parts never used by inventor were taken as attempts to cloud the description; Savory v. Price and similar findings support this presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: If several things are claimed and one is not new the whole may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is taken out for several things to be produced and one of them is not new, the whole patent can be held void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Brunton, others) shows that claiming multiple distinct articles or effects where one is old can render the grant void; courts analyze whether the alleged distinct items are really part of a single invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: If different claimed things include one that fails to produce the claimed effect, careful judgment required
rubrics_metrics.description: If one claimed thing is later found not useful, courts have been reluctant to void the patent altogether unless the specification misled the public or presented the item as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lewis v. Marling and related cases: if a part was claimed but not described as essential and was initially thought necessary, later disuse may not void the patent; context and presentation matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: The description must not give effects that cannot accurately be produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee should inform the inquirer of the exact nature of the manufacture; claiming results that cannot be produced is fatal to the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have invalidated patents where the product or results described in the specification did not in fact have the qualities or effects asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/models: annex where helpful but specification should stand alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A model, diagram, picture, or drawing is generally annexed to illustrate parts of a machine, but if the subject is clearly described the drawing may be omitted; the specification ought to be sufficiently descriptive without needing the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically scales and precise dimensions were required; modern rule: if a common mechanic can make the invention from a perspective drawing and the words, absence of scale is acceptable. Drawings may be used to explain words; if the drawing enables construction it can be as good as written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words should be apt and intelligible to mechanics; cannot rely solely on drawings as a substitute for clear wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be in apt words intelligible to mechanics; although drawings can aid, the words and drawings together must explain each other sufficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bloxam v. Elsee: foreign words in the text were held immaterial because drawings + comparison of words and drawings enabled a skilled mechanic to perform the work; but reliance solely on drawings with meaningless words is risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of general language is contextual and limited to what practical men then considered usable
rubrics_metrics.description: General statements of applicability are read in light of the specification and the practical knowledge at the time; patentees are not required to foresee future successful speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Tenterden: terms like 'other substances' should be understood as substances then known to be suitable; courts will not extend a patentee's description to cover later-discovered uses unless the specification supported that breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against inventor who discontinues previously used parts without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: If parts once fairly introduced are later abandoned, the patentee may omit them, but until he gives a good reason for discontinuance the presumption is against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether parts were genuinely abandoned due to later discoveries or were included initially to mislead; inventor bears burden to explain discontinuance.
